column1: # The FFI bench gate record: one line per check, the target it runs on, the
# .tono it compiles, and the outcome scripts/check-ffi-bench.sh must observe.
# A check that ends elsewhere than recorded fails the gate, in both
# directions: a regression on a green row, and a red row that starts passing
# (update this record and README.md together, that is the progress report).
# outcome: pass | frontend-red | check-red | gen-red | build-red | test-red | run-red | refused
# 02: the handle is held as the concrete type the Rust block spells, and the
# trait method is reached through its own path, which is what brings the
# 07: the options form's Rust block names the library's own type and spells
# the field as Option<u8>, so the literal wraps the value in Some(..).
# 11: the callee is the foreign type itself (FormulaCalculator.parse); Go has
# no static method and nothing to refuse: its block writes the package
# 12: the call passes a declared handle's class itself (instantiate(AnswerCalculator));
# Rust and Go have no type as a value, so their rows pass by being refused.
# 13: the library's Client shares its name with the generated entry's; the
# spelling is the library's and keeps the package selector either way.
# 14: a generated type inside a spelling is referenced by its own name
# (`Memo[.reading]`), never found by matching a word against the module.
# 15: an argument that must convert at the boundary (an i64 into a narrower
# numeric parameter): TypeScript converts across the bigint divide
# (Number(..)), Go writes its builtin conversion (int(..)), and Rust has no
# implicit numeric narrowing, so its generation refuses the binding naming
# 16: the constructor takes a pointer to its options struct. The argument
# spells the crossing (`options { .. }: #(&Options)`) and the form's block
# keeps the plain type, so the form's own probe and the call site compile
# together (a `&` on the block satisfied the call and broke the probe).
